title: Va'etchanan: and I pleaded (Deuteronomy 3:23–26)
hook: Moses begs to enter the land and hears "Let it suffice thee"
tomorrow: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a strong people walked past Edom and Moab and paid for its water. Your line was pass by gently. What did you leave alone? Today a new portion opens, with Moses asking for something he won't get. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

Forty years of work. Every crisis carried. And now, with the finish line in sight, close enough to see the far bank of the river, the word comes: you won't cross it. Someone else will. Moses knew this already; it was decided back at the rock in Numbers. But in his farewell he tells his people something they may not have known: that he went back and asked. He begged. The new portion takes its name from that begging.
screen: `FORTY YEARS, AND THE FAR BANK IN SIGHT.` → `SOMEONE ELSE WILL CROSS.` → `HE WENT BACK AND ASKED.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the old Jewish translation: "And I besought the LORD at that time, saying." The Hebrew first word is va'etchanan, and I pleaded, from the root for grace or favor. Rashi hears in it a request for a free gift, something not earned. And what he asks is simple: "Let me go over, I pray Thee, and see the good land." Just let me see it. The rabbis noticed how hard he asked. A midrash counts the letters of va'etchanan as numbers, and they add up to five hundred fifteen, so the midrash says Moses prayed five hundred fifteen prayers to enter. Then the answer: "Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto Me of this matter." In Hebrew, rav lach. Literally, much to you, or enough for you. It's a no. A final one. But it isn't silent, and it isn't the end of the conversation. In the next breath God tells him to climb to the top of Pisgah and look west, north, south and east, and see the land with his eyes. And to strengthen Joshua, who will lead them across. Rashi hears more than a refusal in rav lach: much good, he says, is already stored up for you. The portion is read on the Sabbath right after Tisha B'Av, called the Sabbath of comfort. The comfort starts with a man who heard no, and still climbed the mountain to look.
screen: `VA'ETCHANAN: AND I PLEADED.` · `LET ME SEE THE GOOD LAND.` · `FIVE HUNDRED FIFTEEN PRAYERS.` · `RAV LACH: LET IT SUFFICE THEE.` · then, large: `LET IT SUFFICE THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one no gracefully. Settle, and breathe. Think of a no you've been given lately. A job, an answer, a body that won't do what it used to, a person who said not now. Let yourself feel how much you wanted it. Then say the two words softly: rav lach. Enough for you. Look around at what is already yours, the way Moses looked out from the mountain. Name three things you can see from where you stand. The bell holds the time.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. Moses' first word in this portion, asking for grace he knows he can't demand.
Your line: let it suffice thee. Today, when a no comes, let it be enough, and look at what you still have. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Va'etchanan is read in synagogues on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, known as Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath of comfort, named for the prophetic reading from Isaiah that follows it.

original.note: Hebrew: and I pleaded, from the root for grace or favor. its letters add up to 515.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses accepted that he wouldn't cross.
what it means: he pleaded, was told rav lach, enough, and then climbed to look at what he wouldn't enter.
what a scholar hears: the midrash reads the gematria of va'etchanan, 515, as the number of his prayers.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the 'you have much already' reading of rav lach is now attributed to Rashi in his own terms (much good is stored up for you) instead of an unattributed expansion; the grace/free-gift sense of va'etchanan attributed to Rashi; hook recast so it doesn't tell the listener what they've done.
Deuteronomy 3:23, 3:25 and 3:26 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify capitalization ('Thee', 'Me') and punctuation.
Gematria of va'etchanan = 515 (vav 6, alef 1, tav 400, chet 8, nun 50, nun 50) and the 515 prayers: Deuteronomy Rabbah 11:10 (also cited in Sifrei); confirm the source.
The reading of rav lach as 'you have much' is a commentators' reading (e.g., Rashi mentions 'much more is stored for you'); confirm attribution before naming anyone.
The decree that Moses wouldn't enter is in Numbers 20:12.
